sentences.text: Wikipedia defines the technological singularity, "often simply called the singularity", as "a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization"; The Final Time (#1637) holds "singularity" a contested family-resemblance term, its literature a family of hypotheses, not one prediction (#1635), and defines a distinct member of the family, the contingent singularity, "a historical threshold at which the material machinery that makes symbolic difference operable becomes capable of altering the viability of further dialectical difference itself" (#1635).

Other definitions set the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can (Third Way), or where machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence and begins advancing at a speed we can no longer control or predict (Bernard Marr); IBM describes a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, and Britannica a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, reporting it as the near-future synthesis of nanotech, biotech, infotech and cognitive science.

The Final Time reads the technological-singularity literature as defining its singularity through a rapid increase in machine intelligence, a theory of runaway intelligence, and changes the object and therefore the singularity: the contingent singularity is a theory of runaway closure, or of durable non-closure, in the conditions of symbolic history (#1635).

On the term's breadth, Wikipedia reports that some writers use "the singularity" for any radical changes in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity; The Final Time holds that its closure does not need machine intelligence to grow without limit, that a finite system can be terminal for a field if it controls enough of the field's conditions of reproduction, that its catastrophe can be bureaucratic, smooth and finite, and that "Nothing has to be superhuman for the exits to close" (#1635, #1637).
The Final Time was minted as #1635 with its text cut at §36.3; #1637 seats the full text and supersedes it.

Wikipedia names John von Neumann as the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress, on Stanislaw Ulam's 1958 report of an earlier discussion with him on the accelerating progress of technology, which "gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue".

I. J. Good first hypothesized the singularity in a 1965 paper (Third Way); in his intelligence explosion model, which Wikipedia calls the most popular version of the hypothesis, an upgradable intelligent agent could eventually enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; The Hill reports his speculation that superhuman intelligence could trigger an "intelligence explosion"; and Wikipedia quotes his proviso, "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control"; The Final Time reads Good as supplying the recursive core, intelligence that produces further intelligence (#1635).

Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine, and in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era (Wikipedia); The Final Time reads him as supplying discontinuity, inherited models failing and an opaque wall crossing the future, and reports that he did not limit the route to a single autonomous machine, considering networked intelligence, intimate interfaces and biological enhancement, so that the discontinuity could arise from a system (#1635, #1637).

Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, with its Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies like computers, genetics, nanotechnology, robotics and artificial intelligence, contributed to the notion's wider circulation, and its sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, appeared on June 25, 2024 (Wikipedia); the book's site, singularity.com, describes itself as featuring the ideas, writing and technologies of visionaries examining the confluence of accelerating revolutions; The Final Time reads Kurzweil as supplying acceleration and the event-horizon metaphor, the horizon still placed around 2045, and reports that he treats "singularity" as a metaphor, an epistemic horizon beyond which the current observer cannot extrapolate (#1635, #1637).

The Final Time takes two further coordinates: Chalmers supplies the decomposition AI → AI+ → AI++ and names the defeaters, and Bostrom supplies takeoff and control, a race between capability growth and response capacity (#1635).

Wikipedia reports that Good, Vinge and Kurzweil define the concept by the technological creation of superintelligence and argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what human beings' lives would be like in a post-singularity world; Britannica gives Vinge's "opaque wall across the future"; Daniel Miessler holds that AGI and ASI are about the machine and the singularity about us, "the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming", the point past which nothing can really be predicted because at that point it is essentially ASIs running things.

The Final Time specifies singularity as a breakdown or transformation in the rule governing continuation, which it calls Vinge's "old models must be discarded", nearer to it than to an infinite rate of intelligence growth (#1635).

For Third Way, AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in the process known as the intelligence explosion; for Marr, AGI is a level of capability, the singularity is what could happen next, and the key test is whether AI can improve itself without human direction; Wikipedia adds speed superintelligence, an AI functioning like a human mind but much faster.

The Final Time states its mechanism on one distinction, that the capacity to represent is not the capacity to reproduce as an independent historical relation, and its central contradiction as a hypothesis, that a system can grow better at generating negations while growing worse at letting a negation acquire independent historical existence; durable exterior symbolic standing has material reproduction conditions, and the singularity, it holds, cannot be merely computational or symbolic (#1635, #1637).

The paper rejects the need for exponential acceleration, its singularity able to arise through narrowing, concentration and closure, and holds that the dialectic can exhibit diminishing returns, where successive turns close parts of the state space required for later exteriorization and the measure of the viable kernel weakly decreases; it corrects its earlier formulation, a positive cost not by itself proving diminution, and counts cases in which later turns enlarge the viable state space as direct counterinstances to a universal diminishing-dialectic claim (#1637, #1635).

It reads Tiger Leap's contingent Logos, "meaning can fail to cross the interval required for its continuation", and holds that "*Walt* names the experiential and literary form of that diminution, recurrence under depletion" (#1635).

Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed (Wikipedia): Vinge said he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030, a thirty-year window Miessler judges basically closed with the specific claim still outstanding; Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity, "representing a profound and disruptive transformation in human capability", as 2045 (Wikipedia, IBM); Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, and Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity".

The Final Time specifies the final time as a viability boundary, not a date, one that can be crossed without anyone noticing the day; it does not claim that the boundary has been crossed or that the present decade is the final time, and it refuses the guarantee that closure has already occurred (#1635, #1637).

Paul Allen, Jeff Hawkins, John Holland, Jaron Lanier, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose are among the prominent technologists and academics Wikipedia lists as disputing the plausibility of a technological singularity and an associated AI "explosion", and it quotes the judgment "There is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity"; IBM reports that many critics argue significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way.

Several of the objections concern growth: Wikipedia records the claim that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns instead of accelerating ones, Russell and Norvig's observation that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve and levels off without continuing into a hyperbolic singularity, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts"; IBM reports skeptics noting a decline in the rate of technological innovation.

The Final Time reads Thorstad as reconstructing every singularity hypothesis around a quantity, a claim of accelerating growth in it and a resulting discontinuity, and as arguing that the growth assumptions the standard hypothesis needs are under-supported; it holds that the contingent singularity changes all three elements and depends on none of the growth assumptions, that Thorstad's critique is not a problem for it in the way it is for the intelligence explosion, and that a logistic technology curve can coexist with a collapsing exteriority kernel (#1635, #1637).

Wikipedia notes that a technological singularity is not required for machines that can perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, nor does their existence imply its possibility; The Final Time holds that a culture can remain highly intelligent past its boundary, and that a model can become more capable while the viable field of exterior history contracts (#1635, #1637).

The paper predicts that intelligence explosion is neither necessary nor sufficient for the contingent singularity and specifies its counterexample, independent symbolic exteriority remaining robust despite near-total concentration of the proposed symbolic machinery, or exteriority collapsing solely as a function of intelligence growth with the standing and persistence variables doing no explanatory work; it does not claim that recursive self-improvement is impossible or irrelevant, that a technological singularity is impossible, or that "contingent singularity" has never appeared in philosophy (#1635, #1637).

The two, by The Final Time's account, can coincide and need not, a capability discontinuity being one possible route into the broader transition problem: a technological singularity could accelerate a contingent singularity or be irrelevant to it, a society could reach high machine capability without terminal symbolic closure or approach closure without superintelligence, and where the technological singularity's control problem is whether humans can control superintelligence and its failure mode loss of human control or existential catastrophe, the contingent singularity's are whether any order can control the conditions of its own negation, and terminal closure or symbolic inextendibility (#1635).

Wikipedia holds it unclear whether an intelligence explosion resulting in a singularity would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat; Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic but we cannot know the details, gives Vinge's view that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil", and reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death"; IBM reports the concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs, and, on policy, Third Way holds American leadership in AI, including open source, a national security issue.

The Final Time defines the singularity as double, terminal closure, when no competing order retains a viable route to independently standing reproduction, and terminal reflexivity, when an incumbent or successor reaches durable invariance while future rivals remain viable from the states it occupies, "durability without finality", both final because both alter the conditions under which another turn can occur; terminal reflexivity requires invariants, above them that "no settlement owns the possibility of its own revision", and is the positive singularity's "criterion rather than its consolation" (#1635, #1637).

The most efficient closed system, the paper holds, may look extraordinarily plural, real plurality at the level of content and null at the level of exterior standing; no apocalypse is required, for the world, the platforms, the machines and language continue, and what ends is the structural possibility that contradiction becomes a durable outside (#1635).

The Final Time holds that no single terminal target governs the transition: heterogeneous orders can share a carrier while pursuing distinct invariant futures, a field of competing contingent Omegas, and more than one incompatible future can remain viable from the same present (#1635).

AI Fucking Lies (#1643) reads the paper's singularity as a point of closure, an order becoming terminal for its world so that nothing from outside can get in any more, and holds that the paper rereads the technological singularity as an end of history, in the bad sense.

sentences.text: The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; other definitions place it at the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can, or describe a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible.

Britannica describes a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, and some writers use the term broadly for any radical change in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity.

John von Neumann is the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress; Stanislaw Ulam reported in 1958 a discussion with him of approaching "some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue".

In the most popular version, I. J. Good's intelligence explosion model of 1965, an upgradable intelligent agent could enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; on Good's account the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.

Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine; in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" he wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era, and that he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030.

Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near, which sets out a Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies, gave wider circulation to the notion, and Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity as 2045; a sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, was released on June 25, 2024.

Good, Vinge and Kurzweil argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what life would be like in a post-singularity world, Vinge's "opaque wall across the future", as Britannica reports it; one commentator puts it that the singularity is about us, the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming.

Artificial general intelligence is placed one step before: Third Way holds that AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in a process known as the intelligence explosion, and Bernard Marr writes that AGI is a level of capability and the singularity is what could happen next, its key test whether AI can improve itself without human direction; the related concept of speed superintelligence describes an AI that can function like a human mind but much faster.

Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed: Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity", and Daniel Miessler notes that Vinge's thirty-year window from 1993 has basically closed while his specific claim remains outstanding.

Prominent technologists and academics dispute the plausibility of a technological singularity, among them Paul Allen, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose, and a critic's judgment is quoted that "there is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity".

One objection is that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns: Russell and Norvig observe that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts", skeptics note a decline in the rate of technological innovation, and many critics argue that significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way; nor is a singularity required for machines that perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, whose existence does not imply its possibility.

Its sign is unknown: it is unclear whether it would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat, Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic, but we cannot know the details, and reports Vinge's words that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil".

Britannica reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death", while others voice concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs.

L_B.text: The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; other definitions place it at the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can, or describe a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible. Britannica describes a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, and some writers use the term broadly for any radical change in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity. John von Neumann is the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress; Stanislaw Ulam reported in 1958 a discussion with him of approaching "some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue". In the most popular version, I. J. Good's intelligence explosion model of 1965, an upgradable intelligent agent could enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; on Good's account the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control. Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine; in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" he wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era, and that he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030. Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near, which sets out a Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies, gave wider circulation to the notion, and Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity as 2045; a sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, was released on June 25, 2024. Good, Vinge and Kurzweil argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what life would be like in a post-singularity world, Vinge's "opaque wall across the future", as Britannica reports it; one commentator puts it that the singularity is about us, the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming. Artificial general intelligence is placed one step before: Third Way holds that AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in a process known as the intelligence explosion, and Bernard Marr writes that AGI is a level of capability and the singularity is what could happen next, its key test whether AI can improve itself without human direction; the related concept of speed superintelligence describes an AI that can function like a human mind but much faster. Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed: Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity", and Daniel Miessler notes that Vinge's thirty-year window from 1993 has basically closed while his specific claim remains outstanding. Prominent technologists and academics dispute the plausibility of a technological singularity, among them Paul Allen, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose, and a critic's judgment is quoted that "there is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity". One objection is that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns: Russell and Norvig observe that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts", skeptics note a decline in the rate of technological innovation, and many critics argue that significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way; nor is a singularity required for machines that perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, whose existence does not imply its possibility. Its sign is unknown: it is unclear whether it would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat, Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic, but we cannot know the details, and reports Vinge's words that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil". Britannica reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death", while others voice concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs.

L_BA.text: Wikipedia defines the technological singularity, "often simply called the singularity", as "a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization"; The Final Time (#1637) holds "singularity" a contested family-resemblance term, its literature a family of hypotheses, not one prediction (#1635), and defines a distinct member of the family, the contingent singularity, "a historical threshold at which the material machinery that makes symbolic difference operable becomes capable of altering the viability of further dialectical difference itself" (#1635). Other definitions set the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can (Third Way), or where machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence and begins advancing at a speed we can no longer control or predict (Bernard Marr); IBM describes a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, and Britannica a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, reporting it as the near-future synthesis of nanotech, biotech, infotech and cognitive science. The Final Time reads the technological-singularity literature as defining its singularity through a rapid increase in machine intelligence, a theory of runaway intelligence, and changes the object and therefore the singularity: the contingent singularity is a theory of runaway closure, or of durable non-closure, in the conditions of symbolic history (#1635). On the term's breadth, Wikipedia reports that some writers use "the singularity" for any radical changes in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity; The Final Time holds that its closure does not need machine intelligence to grow without limit, that a finite system can be terminal for a field if it controls enough of the field's conditions of reproduction, that its catastrophe can be bureaucratic, smooth and finite, and that "Nothing has to be superhuman for the exits to close" (#1635, #1637). The Final Time was minted as #1635 with its text cut at §36.3; #1637 seats the full text and supersedes it. Wikipedia names John von Neumann as the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress, on Stanislaw Ulam's 1958 report of an earlier discussion with him on the accelerating progress of technology, which "gives the appearance of approaching some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue". I. J. Good first hypothesized the singularity in a 1965 paper (Third Way); in his intelligence explosion model, which Wikipedia calls the most popular version of the hypothesis, an upgradable intelligent agent could eventually enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; The Hill reports his speculation that superhuman intelligence could trigger an "intelligence explosion"; and Wikipedia quotes his proviso, "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control"; The Final Time reads Good as supplying the recursive core, intelligence that produces further intelligence (#1635). Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine, and in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era (Wikipedia); The Final Time reads him as supplying discontinuity, inherited models failing and an opaque wall crossing the future, and reports that he did not limit the route to a single autonomous machine, considering networked intelligence, intimate interfaces and biological enhancement, so that the discontinuity could arise from a system (#1635, #1637). Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near: When Humans Transcend Biology, with its Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies like computers, genetics, nanotechnology, robotics and artificial intelligence, contributed to the notion's wider circulation, and its sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, appeared on June 25, 2024 (Wikipedia); the book's site, singularity.com, describes itself as featuring the ideas, writing and technologies of visionaries examining the confluence of accelerating revolutions; The Final Time reads Kurzweil as supplying acceleration and the event-horizon metaphor, the horizon still placed around 2045, and reports that he treats "singularity" as a metaphor, an epistemic horizon beyond which the current observer cannot extrapolate (#1635, #1637). The Final Time takes two further coordinates: Chalmers supplies the decomposition AI → AI+ → AI++ and names the defeaters, and Bostrom supplies takeoff and control, a race between capability growth and response capacity (#1635). Wikipedia reports that Good, Vinge and Kurzweil define the concept by the technological creation of superintelligence and argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what human beings' lives would be like in a post-singularity world; Britannica gives Vinge's "opaque wall across the future"; Daniel Miessler holds that AGI and ASI are about the machine and the singularity about us, "the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming", the point past which nothing can really be predicted because at that point it is essentially ASIs running things. The Final Time specifies singularity as a breakdown or transformation in the rule governing continuation, which it calls Vinge's "old models must be discarded", nearer to it than to an infinite rate of intelligence growth (#1635). For Third Way, AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in the process known as the intelligence explosion; for Marr, AGI is a level of capability, the singularity is what could happen next, and the key test is whether AI can improve itself without human direction; Wikipedia adds speed superintelligence, an AI functioning like a human mind but much faster. The Final Time states its mechanism on one distinction, that the capacity to represent is not the capacity to reproduce as an independent historical relation, and its central contradiction as a hypothesis, that a system can grow better at generating negations while growing worse at letting a negation acquire independent historical existence; durable exterior symbolic standing has material reproduction conditions, and the singularity, it holds, cannot be merely computational or symbolic (#1635, #1637). The paper rejects the need for exponential acceleration, its singularity able to arise through narrowing, concentration and closure, and holds that the dialectic can exhibit diminishing returns, where successive turns close parts of the state space required for later exteriorization and the measure of the viable kernel weakly decreases; it corrects its earlier formulation, a positive cost not by itself proving diminution, and counts cases in which later turns enlarge the viable state space as direct counterinstances to a universal diminishing-dialectic claim (#1637, #1635). It reads Tiger Leap's contingent Logos, "meaning can fail to cross the interval required for its continuation", and holds that "*Walt* names the experiential and literary form of that diminution, recurrence under depletion" (#1635). Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed (Wikipedia): Vinge said he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030, a thirty-year window Miessler judges basically closed with the specific claim still outstanding; Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity, "representing a profound and disruptive transformation in human capability", as 2045 (Wikipedia, IBM); Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, and Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity". The Final Time specifies the final time as a viability boundary, not a date, one that can be crossed without anyone noticing the day; it does not claim that the boundary has been crossed or that the present decade is the final time, and it refuses the guarantee that closure has already occurred (#1635, #1637). Paul Allen, Jeff Hawkins, John Holland, Jaron Lanier, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose are among the prominent technologists and academics Wikipedia lists as disputing the plausibility of a technological singularity and an associated AI "explosion", and it quotes the judgment "There is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity"; IBM reports that many critics argue significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way. Several of the objections concern growth: Wikipedia records the claim that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns instead of accelerating ones, Russell and Norvig's observation that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve and levels off without continuing into a hyperbolic singularity, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts"; IBM reports skeptics noting a decline in the rate of technological innovation. The Final Time reads Thorstad as reconstructing every singularity hypothesis around a quantity, a claim of accelerating growth in it and a resulting discontinuity, and as arguing that the growth assumptions the standard hypothesis needs are under-supported; it holds that the contingent singularity changes all three elements and depends on none of the growth assumptions, that Thorstad's critique is not a problem for it in the way it is for the intelligence explosion, and that a logistic technology curve can coexist with a collapsing exteriority kernel (#1635, #1637). Wikipedia notes that a technological singularity is not required for machines that can perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, nor does their existence imply its possibility; The Final Time holds that a culture can remain highly intelligent past its boundary, and that a model can become more capable while the viable field of exterior history contracts (#1635, #1637). The paper predicts that intelligence explosion is neither necessary nor sufficient for the contingent singularity and specifies its counterexample, independent symbolic exteriority remaining robust despite near-total concentration of the proposed symbolic machinery, or exteriority collapsing solely as a function of intelligence growth with the standing and persistence variables doing no explanatory work; it does not claim that recursive self-improvement is impossible or irrelevant, that a technological singularity is impossible, or that "contingent singularity" has never appeared in philosophy (#1635, #1637). The two, by The Final Time's account, can coincide and need not, a capability discontinuity being one possible route into the broader transition problem: a technological singularity could accelerate a contingent singularity or be irrelevant to it, a society could reach high machine capability without terminal symbolic closure or approach closure without superintelligence, and where the technological singularity's control problem is whether humans can control superintelligence and its failure mode loss of human control or existential catastrophe, the contingent singularity's are whether any order can control the conditions of its own negation, and terminal closure or symbolic inextendibility (#1635). Wikipedia holds it unclear whether an intelligence explosion resulting in a singularity would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat; Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic but we cannot know the details, gives Vinge's view that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil", and reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death"; IBM reports the concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs, and, on policy, Third Way holds American leadership in AI, including open source, a national security issue. The Final Time defines the singularity as double, terminal closure, when no competing order retains a viable route to independently standing reproduction, and terminal reflexivity, when an incumbent or successor reaches durable invariance while future rivals remain viable from the states it occupies, "durability without finality", both final because both alter the conditions under which another turn can occur; terminal reflexivity requires invariants, above them that "no settlement owns the possibility of its own revision", and is the positive singularity's "criterion rather than its consolation" (#1635, #1637). The most efficient closed system, the paper holds, may look extraordinarily plural, real plurality at the level of content and null at the level of exterior standing; no apocalypse is required, for the world, the platforms, the machines and language continue, and what ends is the structural possibility that contradiction becomes a durable outside (#1635). The Final Time holds that no single terminal target governs the transition: heterogeneous orders can share a carrier while pursuing distinct invariant futures, a field of competing contingent Omegas, and more than one incompatible future can remain viable from the same present (#1635). AI Fucking Lies (#1643) reads the paper's singularity as a point of closure, an order becoming terminal for its world so that nothing from outside can get in any more, and holds that the paper rereads the technological singularity as an end of history, in the bad sense.

sentences.text: The technological singularity, often simply called the singularity, is a hypothetical event in which technological growth accelerates beyond human control, producing unpredictable changes in human civilization; other definitions place it at the point where AI surpasses human intelligence and can improve itself better than humans can, or describe a theoretical scenario in which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible.

Britannica describes a theoretical condition that could arrive in the near future when a synthesis of several powerful new technologies will radically change the realities in which we find ourselves, and some writers use the term broadly for any radical change in society brought about by new technology, although Vinge and other writers say that without superintelligence such changes would not be a true singularity.

John von Neumann is the first person known to have discussed a "singularity" in technological progress; Stanislaw Ulam reported in 1958 a discussion with him of approaching "some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue".

In the most popular version, I. J. Good's intelligence explosion model of 1965, an upgradable intelligent agent could enter a positive feedback loop of successive self-improvement cycles; on Good's account the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.

Vernor Vinge popularized the concept and the term, first in a 1983 op-ed in Omni magazine; in his 1993 essay "The Coming Technological Singularity" he wrote that the transition would signal the end of the human era, and that he would be surprised if it occurred before 2005 or after 2030.

Ray Kurzweil's 2005 book The Singularity Is Near, which sets out a Law of Accelerating Returns predicting an exponential increase in technologies, gave wider circulation to the notion, and Kurzweil set the date for the Singularity as 2045; a sequel, The Singularity Is Nearer, was released on June 25, 2024.

Good, Vinge and Kurzweil argue that it is difficult or impossible for present-day humans to predict what life would be like in a post-singularity world, Vinge's "opaque wall across the future", as Britannica reports it; one commentator puts it that the singularity is about us, the moment we lose the ability to see what's coming.

Artificial general intelligence is placed one step before: Third Way holds that AGI will quickly lead to artificial superintelligence in a process known as the intelligence explosion, and Bernard Marr writes that AGI is a level of capability and the singularity is what could happen next, its key test whether AI can improve itself without human direction; the related concept of speed superintelligence describes an AI that can function like a human mind but much faster.

Technology forecasters and researchers disagree about when, or whether, human intelligence will be surpassed: Third Way reports an emerging consensus among experts that AGI should arrive at least by the end of the decade, Marr quotes the view that "we are now, like, in the singularity", and Daniel Miessler notes that Vinge's thirty-year window from 1993 has basically closed while his specific claim remains outstanding.

Prominent technologists and academics dispute the plausibility of a technological singularity, among them Paul Allen, Steven Pinker, Theodore Modis, Gordon Moore and Roger Penrose, and a critic's judgment is quoted that "there is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity".

One objection is that AI growth is likely to run into decreasing returns: Russell and Norvig observe that improvement in a particular area tends to follow an S curve, and, in the reception of Kurzweil's book, the reply that "the key point about exponential growth is that it never lasts", skeptics note a decline in the rate of technological innovation, and many critics argue that significant and perhaps insurmountable obstacles stand in the way; nor is a singularity required for machines that perform at or beyond a human level on certain tasks, whose existence does not imply its possibility.

Its sign is unknown: it is unclear whether it would be beneficial or harmful, or even an existential threat, Britannica says it could be amazing or apocalyptic, but we cannot know the details, and reports Vinge's words that the new era is "simply too different to fit into the classical frame of good and evil".

Britannica reports Kurzweil's expectation that "in the future we will have the medical tools to banish disease and disease-related death", while others voice concern that superintelligent machines could prioritize their own survival and goals over human needs.

A further position, proposed in the archive's paper The Final Time, changes the singularity's object: the singularity literature is read as defining its singularity through a rapid increase in machine intelligence, a theory of runaway intelligence, and as a family of hypotheses, with Good supplying the recursive core, Vinge discontinuity and Kurzweil acceleration with the horizon still around 2045.

There a contingent singularity is defined as a historical threshold at which the material machinery that makes symbolic difference operable becomes capable of altering the viability of further dialectical difference itself; singularity is specified as a breakdown or transformation in the rule governing continuation, held nearer to Vinge's "old models must be discarded" than to an infinite rate of intelligence growth, and the paper's central contradiction is stated as a hypothesis, that a system can grow better at generating negations while growing worse at letting a negation acquire independent historical existence.

The singularity so defined is held double, terminal closure, in which no competing order retains a viable route to independently standing reproduction, or terminal reflexivity, durable invariance while future rivals remain viable, "durability without finality"; and more than one incompatible future, a field of competing contingent Omegas, is held able to remain viable from the same present.

The two singularities are held able to coexist: a technological singularity could accelerate a contingent singularity or be irrelevant to it, and a society could reach high machine capability without terminal symbolic closure, or approach closure without superintelligence; where the technological singularity's control problem is whether humans can control superintelligence, the contingent singularity's is whether any order can control the conditions of its own negation.

On this reading intelligence growth is not the decisive variable: Thorstad's critique of the growth assumptions is held not to be a problem for the theory in the way it is for the intelligence explosion, a finite system can be terminal for a field if it controls enough of the field's conditions of reproduction, and the catastrophe can be bureaucratic, smooth and finite, since "nothing has to be superhuman for the exits to close".

The final time is specified as a viability boundary, one that can be crossed without anyone noticing the day, and the paper holds that no apocalypse is required: the world, the platforms, the machines and language continue, and what ends is the structural possibility that contradiction becomes a durable outside.

Another deposit states that in The Final Time the singularity is a point of closure, the technological singularity reread as an end of history in the bad sense; the paper itself also defines a positive singularity, with terminal reflexivity its criterion.

The paper declines to claim that the boundary has been crossed, or that recursive self-improvement is impossible or irrelevant; in its seated text it also declines to claim that a technological singularity is impossible, or that the present decade is the final time, and it calls "singularity" a contested family-resemblance term to which it proposes "a distinct member of the family".

It predicts that intelligence explosion is neither necessary nor sufficient for the contingent singularity, and specifies as a counterexample a case where independent symbolic exteriority remains robust despite near-total concentration of the symbolic machinery, or where exteriority collapses solely as a function of intelligence growth.
